doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

chapter: Mingus, road life and the jazz economy
title: Overseas reception and jazz work following the economy
summary: Audiences abroad know his career better; jazz interest comes and goes and musicians work according to the economy.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Cool. The reception you get overseas, I’ve heard it’s pretty good for jazz musicians when they go overseas. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

It is. I love — they seem to know more about my career, what I’ve done, things that I’ve forgotten about. Even in Japan it’s like that. I’m sorry to say it’s not like that here. But it seems as though — maybe it’s just this period we’re going through with all this, with the film going on on Channel 13 and that whole series and the IMJK—
Right, whatever this thing in that’s going on here. The thousands of people.
How do you feel about the — I’m not sure how to ask this question, but does the interest and the educational component that’s going on, does it filter down for the musicians in work?

Yeah. It might not last too long. It’s just like when the festivals come in town. It seems like everybody’s working. All the little joints in town, they have some, they’re a part of it. And then it kind of dies down for a while. Actually, I think jazz musicians work according to the economy. I mean it’s just that wide a thing. We’re the first ones to be put out of work when the things start getting a little tight.
Yeah. People stop going out as much?
It seems like it’s an expensive proposition to go out and hear jazz sometimes.
